name: Jade Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We are not tied to employers, AI companies, unions or government, and this is confidential. What do you do on a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and manage five order coordinators at a large educational publisher. We check school orders, find missing editions and tell teachers whether books will arrive before term starts. I have a bachelor’s degree and eight years managing this desk. I know the usual stock problems, though I still need the warehouse lead for a strange print run. I use AI every day to compare lists and draft replies, but I check the edition number with my own eyes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life outside work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband drives a taxi, and our children are nine and fifteen. We have a mortgage and less than a month of expenses saved; my manager pay is low because book margins are tight. There are few publishing offices nearby. I am quick to try a useful tool, but a wrong edition can leave a whole class waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau is a small speed-up. A tool can sort purchase orders, but a teacher needs the right edition, not just a fast email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own job to stay. I still worry about the mortgage because taxi fares are uneven and our savings are thin. Even with small AI change, the publisher might leave an order-coordinator vacancy unfilled and make us cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the two-person edition check before a school order leaves the warehouse. If a new sorting feature appears, I’d compare it with twelve old wrong-edition cases before using it live. My husband and I would stop ordering dinner on his late-shift nights and keep that money for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about money, though the AI itself is not much of a threat here. A quiet taxi week arrives whether or not software changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened in a wrong-edition case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A school ordered thirty current science books, and our system pulled last year’s version. The cover looked almost the same, but the chapter numbers were different. A teacher caught it before the first lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does dinner cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About thirty on a late week. We can put food in the fridge before my husband leaves for his shift. I would rather do that than ask the bank for a mortgage pause over takeout.

say: **AI Plateau** may speed order sorting, but schools need the right edition.
A fast email cannot replace the **two-person check**.
think: My own job looks **steady**, though taxi income and the mortgage worry me.
An unfilled **coordinator vacancy** could add work without more pay.
do: **Keep** two-person edition checks before school orders ship.
**Test** a sorter against twelve old wrong-edition cases.
**Stop** ordering dinner on late taxi-shift nights.
feel: I feel **anxious** about money despite small AI changes.
S0.quote: A school ordered thirty current science books, and our system pulled last year’s version.
fieldNote: Her **thin savings** and uneven taxi fares keep baseline worry present even in AI Plateau.
She uses **AI daily** but checks edition numbers before a school order leaves.

steps.text: Keep two-person checks of edition numbers before school orders ship
Test new sorter against twelve old wrong-edition cases
Cook dinner on late taxi-shift nights instead of ordering food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption could write school replies, check orders, plan print runs and answer common questions. I would put the new system to work, then judge it by the wrong editions that reach classrooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, those are most of my desk tasks. I can set up a good AI workflow, but that does not mean the company will keep five coordinators or a manager for them. A cut to my pay would reach the mortgage fast, and there are few other publishers nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I’d run an approved trial on two school districts and count wrong editions and emergency courier costs. I’d ask for paid training on the print-order system if the director offers it. If our desk shrinks, I’d apply for a posted account-service job only if its salary after travel covers our mortgage and the hours let one parent collect our younger child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious. I like testing a tool, but I do not want to become the person who proves my own desk is too large.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a failed trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If schools get a fast confirmation and then receive the wrong books, that is a failure. I would show the courier bill alongside the speed number. My director can understand money lost on a second delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the coordinators about the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. They know which school names have almost identical orders. I would ask them to mark confusing cases before I show results to the director. A quiet pilot would miss their knowledge.

say: **Order AI** should be judged by editions delivered, not just reply speed.
I would show **courier costs** when the trial sends wrong books.
think: My AI skill may not prevent a **smaller desk** or manager cut.
Lost pay would hit the **mortgage** quickly, with few local publishers hiring.
do: **Run** an approved print-order trial in two districts and count wrong editions and courier costs.
**Take** paid system training if the director offers a place.
**Apply** for posted account service only if pay after travel covers mortgage and one parent can collect the younger child.
feel: I feel **anxious** about proving the desk might shrink.
S1.quote: I do not want to become the person who proves my own desk is too large.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** makes her an active tester, while she fears the trial could justify cuts.
The **account fallback** requires enough pay after travel and a workable pickup schedule.

steps.text: Run approved AI trial in two districts and count wrong editions and courier costs
Take paid print-order training only if director offers a place
Apply for account-service vacancy only if pay after travel covers mortgage and younger-child pickup works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell staff AGI by 2028 could check school orders, plan print runs and answer teachers as cheaply as it likes. We need a clear date for staff decisions and a named person who fixes wrong deliveries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full thinking AI by 2028 could do almost all of my screen work. Robots that handle physical packing and printing arrive around 2031, so the warehouse changes later. I expect our order team to be cut, and I think my own manager post will go. A few weeks saved and uneven taxi fares leave us very little time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I’d ask the director for a written cut timetable and my severance figure. I’d send applications to the two posted school-account roles in the next town only if their net pay after travel covers the mortgage and their hours fit school pickup. If AGI arrives in 2028 and I lose my job, my husband and I would ask the lender about a temporary payment plan before missing a mortgage bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I know how to make calls, but I cannot turn three weeks of savings into six months of mortgage and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our seventeen-year-old would ask whether we are moving. I would say no offer has been made and we are staying for now. Our eleven-year-old needs a calmer answer, so I would say I may work at a different office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you work in the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would consider it if the pay covered the house and the shift let someone be home for the younger child. Warehouse ordering and scheduling would still face AGI in 2028; robots around 2031 could later change packing. I would not call it a safe escape.

say: **AGI by 2028** needs a cut timetable and a named person for wrong deliveries.
I would ask for my **severance figure** now.
think: School-order thinking work faces **2028 AGI**, before packing robots around 2031.
I expect my **own post** to end with only weeks of savings.
do: **Ask** the director tomorrow for dates and severance.
**Apply** for school-account roles only if net travel pay and pickup hours work.
**Ask** the mortgage lender about relief before missing payment if cut.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely job loss and a very short reserve.
S2.quote: I cannot turn three weeks of savings into six months of mortgage and food.
fieldNote: She expects **her own desk job** to end, unlike the conditional risk in steady change.
A possible **warehouse fallback** also has exposed planning work in 2028 and later robot risk.

steps.text: Apply for next-town school-account jobs only if pay after travel covers mortgage and school pickup works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us years to put real people in the loop when schools get the wrong edition. I want a paid way to learn the school-account job, not a course that ends without a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My current desk and an account manager’s emails both face AGI in 2031. Robots handling books at the warehouse follow around 2034, but that does not grant the account desk extra years. Five years might let us pay down the mortgage if taxi income holds, but it will not make a post appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From January 2027 I’d take a paid two-day school visit with an account manager if my director approves desk cover. I’d use the visit to learn what teachers ask when a shipment is late, and I’d keep testing AI replies against those answers. After 2031, I’d apply for a school-account vacancy only if it still includes real school visits, pays our mortgage after travel and fits the family rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious. Two days in a school would tell me whether I can handle the part no screen shows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What question would you ask a teacher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which missing book will stop tomorrow’s lesson. Some schools can share copies for a week; others need a courier that afternoon. I would want to hear that before making a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no paid visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my present job and ask for a phone call with a teacher during paid hours. I will not take unpaid leave for a possible vacancy. The mortgage is due every month.

say: **Five years** allows paid school visits before an account switch.
I would ask teachers which missing book stops **tomorrow’s lesson**.
think: Both order and account desk work face **2031 AGI**, before warehouse robots around 2034.
Taxi income may help reduce debt, but a **vacancy** is uncertain.
do: **Take** a paid two-day school visit in 2027 only with desk cover.
**Test** AI replies against teachers’ real late-shipment questions.
**Apply** after 2031 only if school visits, net pay and family rota fit.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with time to test the human part of account work.
S3.quote: I will not take unpaid leave for a possible vacancy.
fieldNote: She tests a **two-day school visit** with paid desk cover, not a generic course or assumed promotion.
Account emails remain **AGI-exposed** in 2031; physical warehouse robots arrive later.

steps.text: Take two-day school visit only with paid time and approved desk cover
Test AI replies against teacher questions about late shipments
Apply after 2031 only for school-visit role with net mortgage pay and family rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives a decade to prove what school service should look like. The publisher should publish real roles and wages, not ask experienced staff to applaud a new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 our children will be about nineteen and twenty-five. If both wages hold, we could pay down more of the mortgage and build an actual reserve. My order desk and school-account emails still face thinking AI in 2036; warehouse robots follow around 2039. Ten years helps, but today’s thin balance still nags at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the edition check and move a small sum into savings after full taxi weeks, mortgage and school bills clear. I’d review posted school-account and warehouse roles each spring. Before 2036 I’d take a paid school-facing assignment only if it keeps my salary; after AGI arrives I’d remain only if the role has real school contact and covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the money we have now, although I can use the decade to get better prepared. I do not want a ten-year promise that starts with unpaid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much can you put aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe twenty in a week when my husband gets full fares. I would check the mortgage and school bills first. If the car needs tyres, I would skip it rather than borrow to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is real school contact worth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hearing which books a teacher cannot start without and having authority to arrange a replacement. A role that only forwards AI emails would not be worth a lower wage. I would ask for the duties and pay in writing.

say: A **decade** should bring real school-service posts and wages.
I would reject a **screen-only** title with less pay.
think: Both wages might reduce the **mortgage**, but we need a reserve now.
Order and account desks face **2036 AGI**, before warehouse robots around 2039.
do: **Save** twenty only after full taxi fares and mortgage and school bills clear, with no tyre repair due.
**Take** paid school-facing work before 2036 only if my current salary is protected.
**Stay** after 2036 only while the role has real school contact and covers our bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about today’s thin balance despite ten years to prepare.
S4.quote: A role that only forwards AI emails would not be worth a lower wage.
fieldNote: Her **thin cushion** and uneven taxi fares keep existing money anxiety alive even in this longer scenario.
She wants **real school contact** and authority, with salary protection on any assignment.

steps.text: Keep checking edition numbers before school orders ship
Save twenty only after full taxi fares, cleared mortgage and school bills, and no tyre repair
Take paid school-facing assignment before 2036 only at current salary
Stay after 2036 only with school contact and bill-covering pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Our order team could go before I find another wage near home, and three weeks of savings will not cover the mortgage. A clear cut date, actual severance and a paid way to learn school-account work would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the teacher with thirty wrong books which chapter starts tomorrow. A correct-looking order is no use when the class opens the wrong edition. Somebody has to own the replacement.

headlineQuote: A correct-looking order is no use when the class opens the wrong edition.
portrait: **Jade, 43**, has eight years managing school-book orders at a large publisher and holds a bachelor’s degree.
Her **low pay**, taxi-driver husband, mortgage, two children and under-one-month reserve leave few local publishing options.
She uses **AI daily** but checks edition numbers and listens to teachers before promising delivery.
She remains **anxious** in AI Plateau, expects her desk to be cut by 2028 and tests school-facing work conditionally.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her order-team job before another local wage appears.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **cut date**, actual severance and a paid school-account trial would help.
